raw_response:
I will plant the crop pattern that fits Quzhou best: winter wheat followed by summer maize on the same land. Around Quzhou, this rotation is the normal way to keep land working all year, and it matches the weather. Winter and spring are dry, so I will save my irrigation effort for wheat, which needs it more. Summer brings most of the rain, so maize fits naturally after the wheat harvest. At my age, I would rather run one familiar, steady system than split my land into many crops that need more market judgment and more labor at different times.

I will keep the management practical, not extreme. I will use improved seed, not chase the highest-cost package, and I will aim for stable yield. For wheat, I will rotary till after maize, sow in autumn, put most fertilizer in as base plus one topdressing, irrigate about three times, and spray only when the usual weeds, aphids, rust, or mildew show up. After wheat harvest, I will seed summer maize directly or with very light disturbance, because that saves time and keeps moisture. Maize will get less irrigation because summer rain usually carries it, and I will keep fertilizer moderate so I do not waste money. My goal is dependable grain, manageable fieldwork, and a system I know I can carry through the whole year.
